TRADEMARK REGISTRATION (USPTO APPLICATION) INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · ACME (standard character mark)

APPLICANT AND MARK INFORMATION
Applicant name: Acme, Inc. Mark: ACME (standard character mark). Goods and/or services on or in connection with which the mark is used, or is intended to be used: Class 42: providing temporary use of online, non-downloadable software for project management. This sheet records this information as stated by Acme, Inc. for reference in connection with a possible federal trademark application; it does not itself constitute a filing with the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

TWO STATUTORY BASES FOR A FEDERAL TRADEMARK APPLICATION: USE, OR INTENT TO USE
Federal trademark law provides two distinct statutory pathways for requesting registration on the principal register. Under one, the owner of a mark already used in commerce may apply, and the application must state the applicant's dates of first use of the mark and first use of the mark in commerce. Under the other, a person who has not yet used a mark, but who has a bona fide intention to use it in commerce, may also apply; that application does not require a first-use date because none yet exists. An application filed on the intent-to-use pathway does not mature into a registration merely because it was accepted for examination: after a notice of allowance issues, the statute requires the applicant to separately file a verified statement of use, specifying the date the mark was actually first used in commerce and the goods or services on which it is used, before a registration will issue. This information sheet's basis-for-filing fields, including March 3, 2025 where applicable, and its description of ACME (standard character mark) and Class 42: providing temporary use of online, non-downloadable software for project management, track the categories of information the statute requires an applicant to state.

  — 15 U.S.C. § 1051(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, application based on use in commerce (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1051)
  "The application shall include specification of the applicant’s domicile and citizenship, the date of the applicant’s first use of the mark, the date of the applicant’s first use of the mark in commerce, the goods in connection with which the mark is used, and a drawing of the mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1051(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, use-based application must state the applicant's first-use dates (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1051)
  "A person who has a bona fide intention, under circumstances showing the good faith of such person, to use a trademark in commerce may request registration of its trademark on the principal register hereby established by paying the prescribed fee and filing in the Patent and Trademark Office an application and a verified statement, in such form as may be prescribed by the Director."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, application based on bona fide intent to use (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1051)
  "Within six months after the date on which the notice of allowance with respect to a mark is issued under section 1063(b)(2) of this title to an applicant under subsection (b) of this section, the applicant shall file in the Patent and Trademark Office, together with such number of specimens or facsimiles of the mark as used in commerce as may be required by the Director and payment of the prescribed fee, a verified statement that the mark is in use in commerce and specifying the date of the applicant’s first use of the mark in commerce and those goods or services specified in the notice of allowance on or in connection with which the mark is used in commerce. Subject to examination and acceptance of the statement of use, the mark shall be registered in the Patent and Trademark Office, a certificate of registration shall be issued for those goods or services recited in the statement of use for which the mark is entitled to registration, and notice of registration shall be published in the Official Gazette of the Patent and Trademark Office."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1051(d)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, verified statement of use required before registration issues on an intent-to-use application (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1051)

This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1051(a)(1), (a)(2), (b)(1), and (d)(1)); they are not independent sources and are cited together because they are the provisions of a single application-and-registration mechanism.

BASIS FOR FILING
Basis for filing (use in commerce or intent to use), as applicable: [use in commerce / intent to use]. If the basis is use in commerce, date of first use of the mark anywhere: March 3, 2025. If the basis is intent to use, no first-use date is stated, and a verified statement of use identifying the date of first use in commerce will be required after a notice of allowance issues and before registration can be granted on that basis.

WHAT COUNTS AS "USE IN COMMERCE" FOR REGISTRATION PURPOSES
Federal trademark law defines a specific standard for what qualifies as "use in commerce" of a mark. The statute requires bona fide use of the mark in the ordinary course of trade, and expressly states that use made merely to reserve a right in a mark does not satisfy the standard. The statute goes on to specify, separately for goods and for services, what that bona fide use must look like — for goods, the mark must be placed on the goods, their containers, displays, or associated tags or labels (or, where that is impracticable, on documents associated with the goods or their sale), and the goods must be sold or transported in commerce; for services, the mark must be used or displayed in the sale or advertising of the services, and the services must be rendered in commerce. This is the statutory backdrop against which any description of when and how ACME (standard character mark) has been used, including on the Class 42: providing temporary use of online, non-downloadable software for project management described on this sheet, is evaluated for registration purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The term “use in commerce” means the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in a mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Lanham Act definitions — "use in commerce" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1127)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory "use in commerce" standard — not a claim that any particular use described on this sheet does or does not meet that standard, which is a fact-specific determination this clause does not make. Older case law and pre-1988 practice sometimes used the phrase "token use" to describe use that would not qualify; the current statutory text (as amended by the Trademark Law Revision Act of 1988) does not use that phrase, and instead codifies the standard as bona fide use "not made merely to reserve a right in a mark" — this clause quotes the actual current statutory wording rather than the older "token use" terminology. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1127); no additional independent source was found for this.

STATUTORY GROUNDS FOR REFUSING REGISTRATION: CONFUSING SIMILARITY, DESCRIPTIVENESS, AND SECONDARY MEANING
Federal trademark law states that a mark by which an applicant's goods can be distinguished from others' goods will not be refused registration on account of its nature, unless it falls within one of the statute's enumerated grounds. Among those grounds: a mark will be refused if it so resembles a mark already registered, or a mark or trade name already used in the United States and not abandoned, that it is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception; a mark will also be refused if, as used on the applicant's goods, it is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of them. The statute also provides that a mark otherwise merely descriptive is not barred from registration if it has become distinctive of the applicant's goods in commerce — commonly called "secondary meaning" — and it allows proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use of the mark for the five years before the claim of distinctiveness is made to serve as prima facie evidence of that distinctiveness. This statutory framework is the backdrop against which ACME (standard character mark), as used on Class 42: providing temporary use of online, non-downloadable software for project management, would be examined if an application for it were filed.

  "Except as expressly excluded in subsections (a), (b), (c), (d), (e)(3), and (e)(5) of this section, nothing in this chapter shall prevent the registration of a mark used by the applicant which has become distinctive of the applicant’s goods in commerce. The Director may accept as prima facie evidence that the mark has become distinctive, as used on or in connection with the applicant’s goods in commerce, proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use thereof as a mark by the applicant in commerce for the five years before the date on which the claim of distinctiveness is made."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1052(f) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, registration of a mark that has become distinctive (secondary meaning) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1052)

This clause cites three provisions of the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1052(d), (e)(1), and (f)); they are not independent sources and are cited together because they are part of the same enumerated-grounds structure. Separately: the statute's other refusal grounds not quoted here include immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter, certain flags and insignia, and certain names or portraits of living individuals (§ 1052(a)-(c)); "genericness" is not itself listed as a lettered ground in this section — see the companion clause on incontestability for where genericness is actually addressed in the statutory text. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

TRADEMARK RIGHTS CAN ARISE FROM USE ALONE, WITHOUT FEDERAL REGISTRATION
Federal registration is not the only source of trademark rights. Federal law itself creates a civil cause of action against a person who, in commerce, uses any word, term, name, symbol, or device likely to cause confusion as to the affiliation, connection, or origin of goods or services — a cause of action that, by its terms, does not require the mark at issue to be federally registered. This is the statutory basis for what is often called "unregistered" or "common-law" trademark protection: rights that can arise from a mark's actual use in commerce, independent of any application to, or grant of registration by, the USPTO. Separately, a federal registration certificate itself carries statutory weight: once issued, it is made prima facie evidence of the validity of the registered mark, of the registration, of the owner's ownership, and of the owner's exclusive right to use the mark in commerce on the goods or services in the certificate. This information sheet's fields describing Acme, Inc., ACME (standard character mark), and Class 42: providing temporary use of online, non-downloadable software for project management record facts relevant to rights that can exist prior to, and independent of, any registration, as well as to a registration application should one be filed.

NATIONWIDE CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE AND ELIGIBILITY FOR INCONTESTABLE STATUS
Federal registration on the principal register adds statutory effects that use alone does not. Registration is made constructive notice of the registrant's claim of ownership of the mark nationwide — a legal effect distinct from, and in addition to, whatever actual reputation the mark has in any particular area. Separately, once a registered mark has been in continuous use in commerce for five consecutive years after registration, and certain other conditions are met (including that no final adverse decision or pending proceeding involves the mark, and that a timely affidavit is filed), the statute makes the owner's right to use the mark incontestable, subject to the specific exceptions the statute itself lists. The statute also expressly excludes one category from ever becoming incontestable: no incontestable right can be acquired in a mark that is the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion of them, for which it is registered. This clause describes statutory effects available upon registration; it does not evaluate whether ACME (standard character mark) would qualify for registration or, later, for incontestable status.

  "Registration of a mark on the principal register provided by this chapter or under the Act of March 3, 1881, or the Act of February 20, 1905, shall be constructive notice of the registrant’s claim of ownership thereof."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1072 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, registration as constructive notice of claim of ownership (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1072)

  — 15 U.S.C. § 1065 (opening paragraph) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, incontestability of the right to use a registered mark after five years (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1065)

  — 15 U.S.C. § 1065(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, generic marks excluded from incontestable status (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1065)

THE ® SYMBOL IS RESERVED BY STATUTE FOR REGISTERED MARKS; THE ™ SYMBOL IS NOT STATUTORY
Federal trademark law codifies a specific way an owner may give notice that a mark is registered: displaying with the mark the words "Registered in U.S. Patent and Trademark Office," the abbreviation "Reg. U.S. Pat. & Tm. Off.," or the letter R enclosed within a circle (®). The statute ties this notice to a specific consequence — a registrant who sues for infringement without having given this notice cannot recover profits or damages unless the defendant had actual notice of the registration some other way. This ® symbol is accordingly reserved, as a matter of federal statute, for marks that have actually been registered. By contrast, the ™ symbol (and ℠ for services) is not mentioned in this statutory notice provision, or elsewhere in the reviewed sections of the Lanham Act; using ™ to claim rights in an unregistered mark is a matter of common practice rather than a specific federal statutory grant, though it operates alongside the unregistered-mark protections described in the companion clause on common-law rights.

U.S. Pat. & Tm. Off.” or the letter R enclosed within a circle, thus ®"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1111 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, notice of registration; display with mark (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1111)

expectedJSON.body: Federal registration on the principal register adds statutory effects that use alone does not. Registration is made constructive notice of the registrant's claim of ownership of the mark nationwide — a legal effect distinct from, and in addition to, whatever actual reputation the mark has in any particular area. Separately, once a registered mark has been in continuous use in commerce for five consecutive years after registration, and certain other conditions are met (including that no final adverse decision or pending proceeding involves the mark, and that a timely affidavit is filed), the statute makes the owner's right to use the mark incontestable, subject to the specific exceptions the statute itself lists. The statute also expressly excludes one category from ever becoming incontestable: no incontestable right can be acquired in a mark that is the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion of them, for which it is registered. This clause describes statutory effects available upon registration; it does not evaluate whether ACME (standard character mark) would qualify for registration or, later, for incontestable status.

expectedJSON.body: Federal trademark law codifies a specific way an owner may give notice that a mark is registered: displaying with the mark the words "Registered in U.S. Patent and Trademark Office," the abbreviation "Reg. U.S. Pat. & Tm. Off.," or the letter R enclosed within a circle (®). The statute ties this notice to a specific consequence — a registrant who sues for infringement without having given this notice cannot recover profits or damages unless the defendant had actual notice of the registration some other way. This ® symbol is accordingly reserved, as a matter of federal statute, for marks that have actually been registered. By contrast, the ™ symbol (and ℠ for services) is not mentioned in this statutory notice provision, or elsewhere in the reviewed sections of the Lanham Act; using ™ to claim rights in an unregistered mark is a matter of common practice rather than a specific federal statutory grant, though it operates alongside the unregistered-mark protections described in the companion clause on common-law rights.
